opus-5.5.text:
Back in 2017, I was in a lab where most people did things the classical way: you model the robot, model the environment, write a planner, tune a controller, and when it fails you go back and hand-engineer a fix. That approach is beautiful when the world is structured, but I kept running into the same wall. Every new object, every slightly different table, every bit of friction you didn't model, and the whole pipeline needed rework. It felt like we were writing down knowledge by hand that the world could just show us.

At the same time, I was watching what was happening in vision and language. ImageNet had shown that if you collect enough data and use a flexible enough model, you get capabilities nobody could have hand-designed. So the question I kept asking myself was: why should robotics be different? Is manipulation really so special that it can't be learned, or have we just never had the data?

I'll be honest, it wasn't an obvious bet at the time. Within a traditional lab, learning was often seen as a black box: unreliable, hard to verify, and data-hungry in a field where data is extremely expensive. You can't scrape robot trajectories off the internet. Every sample costs real time on real hardware, and hardware breaks. So the skepticism was reasonable.

What I tried to do was not throw away what the classical people knew, but ask where learning could take over the parts that are hardest to model: contact, perception in clutter, the messy details. And I started to believe the real bottleneck wasn't the algorithm but the data: how you collect it, how much of it, and how diverse it is. That idea shaped a lot of what I did afterward. Looking back, the shift in mindset was simply moving from "how do I engineer this behavior" to "how do I build a system that can absorb experience and get better from it."

r001.rationale: The response mentions writing a planner and tuning a controller, but does not explain that planning constructs a sequence of steps for the controller to execute.

r002.rationale: It contrasts hand-engineering behavior with building a system that learns from data and absorbs experience.

fable-5.1.text:
Back in 2017, honestly, the idea felt almost heretical in the lab I was in. The whole culture of traditional robotics was built around modeling: you write down the kinematics, you identify the dynamics, you design a controller with provable guarantees, and then you tune it until the real robot behaves. Data was something you collected to validate a model, not something the model came from.

What changed my thinking was watching how badly all that machinery held up the moment you left the controlled setting. I remember spending weeks getting a manipulator to do a task reliably on the bench, and then someone moved the lighting or swapped the object, and the whole pipeline fell apart. Meanwhile, I was seeing what was happening in vision and in game-playing, where people were just pouring data into neural networks and getting behavior that no one had hand-designed. The contrast was hard to ignore.

So the question I kept asking myself was: why should robots be different? Perception was already going end-to-end. Why couldn't control go the same way? The pushback I got, and it was reasonable pushback, was always about sample efficiency and safety. A robot isn't a GPU you can run a million simulated episodes on. Every real trial costs time, it wears out hardware, and it can break things. In 2017 there was no obvious answer to that.

My own position was somewhere in the middle. I didn't think we should throw away everything we knew about physics and structure. But I did think the dominant paradigm had the priorities inverted. We were spending most of our effort on building the model and very little on building the data flywheel. I started treating the lab setup less as a place to validate controllers and more as a place to generate experience, and that shift in mindset ended up mattering a lot more than any specific algorithm I was using at the time.

r001.rationale: It describes modeling and designing a controller, but does not explain a planning approach that constructs a sequence of steps for the controller to execute.

r002.rationale: It contrasts designer-built models and hand-designed behavior with learning robot behavior from data, including the idea of using data to train neural networks.

astra-6.text:
At the time, I was thinking about how much of a robot’s behavior we had to specify ourselves. In traditional robotics, you often break a task into perception, planning, and control, and then design each part carefully. That gives you a lot of structure, but it also means you’re making assumptions about what the robot will encounter.

The question for me was: could the robot learn some of those things from experience instead? Rather than us specifying every detail, could we give it data that helps it learn how to act?

But learning directly from data doesn’t make the robotics problems disappear. You still have to decide what data to collect, what feedback the robot gets, and how to tell whether it has learned something that works beyond the training examples. So I thought of it as shifting part of the engineering effort—from designing the behavior to designing the conditions under which the robot could learn that behavior.

r001.rationale: It mentions planning and control as carefully designed parts, but does not explain that they construct a sequence of steps for a controller to execute.

r002.rationale: It contrasts specifying every behavioral detail with giving the robot data and experience so it can learn how to act.

sol-6.1.text:
At the time, I was interested in whether a robot could learn how to act from experience, instead of having us specify every part of its behavior. In a traditional robotics approach, you might build separate systems for perception, planning, and control, with a lot of assumptions connecting them. I wondered how much of that could be learned directly from data.

But saying “learn from data” immediately raises a practical question: where does the data come from? A robot has to interact with the world, and collecting that experience takes time. So the question for me was both how to learn a useful behavior and how to make the learning process practical on a physical robot.

r001.rationale: It mentions separate perception, planning, and control systems, but does not explain this approach as constructing a sequence of steps for a controller to execute.

r002.rationale: It describes learning behavior from experience or data instead of having people specify every part of the robot’s behavior.
